'''Barbara S. Askins''' (born 1939) is an American [[chemist]]. She is best known for her invention of a method to enhance underexposed photographic [[negative (photography)|negatives]]. This development was used extensively by [[NASA]] and the medical industry, and it earned Askins the title of National Inventor of the Year in 1978.<ref>{{Cite book|title=American Women in Technology|publisher=[[ABC-CLIO]]|year=2000|isbn=1-57607-072-7|editor-last=Zierdt-Warshaw|editor-first=Linda|location=Santa Barbara, California|page=[https://archive.org/details/americanwomenint0000zier/page/19 19]|chapter=Askins, Barbara (n.d.)|editor-last2=Winkler|editor-first2=Alan|editor-last3=Bernstein|editor-first3=Leonard|chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/americanwomenint0000zier/page/19}}</ref>

== Early years, education and early career ==

Askins was born in [[Belfast, Tennessee]], in 1939. She began her career as a teacher. After her two children entered school, Askins returned to college to complete her bachelor's degree in chemistry and earn her master's degree in chemistry. She joined NASA's [[Marshall Space Flight Center]] in 1975.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://lemelson.mit.edu/resources/barbara-askins|title = Barbara Askins &#124; Lemelson}}</ref>

== Research career ==
Askins is a physical chemist who worked for NASA's [[Marshall Space Flight Center]] and is best known for her pioneering invention of a process in which "images on developed photographic [[emulsion]]s can be significantly intensified by making the image silver radioactive and exposing a second emulsion to this radiation."<ref name=Askins>{{cite journal|last1=Askins|first1=Barbara S.|title=Photographic image intensification by autoradiography|journal=Applied Optics|date=1 November 1976|volume=15|issue=11|pages=2860–2865|url=http://www.opticsinfobase.org/ao/abstract.cfm?uri=ao-15-11-2860|access-date=26 June 2014|doi=10.1364/ao.15.002860|pmid=20165502|bibcode=1976ApOpt..15.2860A|url-access=subscription}}</ref> The resulting print, known as an [[autoradiograph]], reproduces the image with significant increases in density and [[contrast (vision)|contrast]]. Her groundbreaking method enhanced underexposed emulsions and increased the limits of photographic detection. In short, it made visible the invisible in photos that would otherwise have been useless. This was very useful for a number of applications, including the coaxing of data from underexposed space images—such as those peering deep into space as well as those highlighting the [[planetary geology|geology]] of other bodies in the [[Solar System]].<ref name=FWI />

Askins' invention also led to significant advances in the field of medical technology. In particular, Askins' method prompted improvements in the development of [[X-ray]] images. Medical images that were 96 percent underexposed suddenly become readable; this meant that doctors could dramatically decrease the amount of X-ray radiation they gave to patients when running routine or emergency tests.<ref name=Stanley>{{cite book|last1=Stanley|first1=Autumn|title=Mothers and daughters of invention: notes for a revised history of technology|date=1993|publisher=[[Rutgers University Press]]|location=New Brunswick, N.J.|isbn=0813521971|pages=574–575}}<!--|accessdate=26 June 2014--></ref> Askins' process was also later used in the restoration of old photographs.<ref name=GRIN /> Askins patented her invention in 1978 (U.S. patent No. 4,101,780),<ref name=patent>{{cite web|title=Patent US4101780 Treating silver with a radioactive sulfur compound such as thiourea or derivatives|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US4101780|website=Google Patents|access-date=26 June 2014}}</ref> and NASA employed it extensively for its research and development work.<ref name=FWI />

==Awards and professional memberships==
In 1978, the Association for Advancement of Inventions and Innovations named Askins the National Inventor of the Year.<ref name=GRIN>{{cite web|title=Great Images in NASA - Barbara Askins, Chemist |url=http://grin.hq.nasa.gov/ABSTRACTS/GPN-2004-00022.html |website=Great Images in NASA |publisher=[[NASA]] |access-date=26 June 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111023221136/http://grin.hq.nasa.gov/ABSTRACTS/GPN-2004-00022.html |archive-date=23 October 2011 }}</ref> She was the first individual woman to earn this honor.<ref name=FWI>{{cite web|title=Barbara Askins: Inventor of a New Film Developing Method|url=http://www.women-inventors.com/Barbara-Askins.asp|website=Famous Women Inventors|access-date=26 June 2014}}</ref>

Askins is a member of the [[American Chemical Society]], the [[Sigma Xi]] honorary research Society, the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]], and the [[World Future Society]].<ref name=Stanley />
